summary.text: Volcanic ash is made of bits of rock, mineral crystals and volcanic glass smaller than 2 mm across, thrown out during volcanic eruptions.
It forms when gases dissolved in magma expand violently and shatter it, or when magma meets water that flashes to steam and breaks the magma apart.
Wind can carry ash thousands of kilometres, so it can harm the health of people and animals, disrupt flights, and damage power, water and transport systems.

facts.label: Broader term
facts.value: Tephra, which includes pieces larger than 2 mm

facts.label: Travel distance
facts.value: Up to thousands of kilometres on the wind

facts.label: Breaking point
facts.value: Bubbles make up about 70–80% of the erupting mixture

facts.label: Basalt ash
facts.value: Dark, about 45–55% silica, rich in iron and magnesium

items.prompt: A geologist picks up a volcanic fragment 5 mm across. Strictly speaking, should it be called volcanic ash?

options.label: No, it is too big to count as ash
Yes, anything a volcano throws out is ash
Yes, as long as it contains volcanic glass
No, ash must be made of pure crystals

items.explain: Ash means fragments under 2 mm; larger pieces belong to the broader group called tephra.

items.prompt: In an explosive eruption, what actually breaks the rising magma into tiny pieces?

options.label: Cold air freezing the magma and cracking it
Dissolved gases expanding violently and tearing it apart
Rocks in the vent grinding the magma down
Lightning in the eruption cloud splitting it

items.explain: Gas bubbles grow as the magma rises, and when they expand violently they rip the magma into fragments that harden into ash.

items.prompt: Hot magma rises into the bottom of a lake. Why can this produce ash?

options.label: The lake water slowly dissolves the magma
The cool water makes the magma crumble gently
The water flashes to steam and shatters the magma
Mud from the lake bed mixes into fine powder

items.explain: Contact with magma turns the water to steam explosively, and that blast breaks the magma into small particles.

items.prompt: A large volcano erupts and its ash rises high into the air. How far can wind carry that ash?

options.label: Only a few hundred metres from the vent
About as far as the volcano's own slopes
Roughly ten kilometres at the very most
Up to thousands of kilometres away

items.explain: Once airborne, ash can travel on the wind for thousands of kilometres, which is why its effects spread so widely.

items.prompt: Dry ash coats the equipment at an electrical substation and causes little trouble. Then a light fog rolls in. What changes?

options.label: Salts on the ash dissolve, so it can carry current
The fog rinses the ash away and ends the risk
The ash sets into a hard, waterproof shell
The damp ash cools down and stops reacting

items.explain: Dry salt crystals on ash mostly insulate, but moisture dissolves them, making the ash corrosive and able to conduct electricity.

items.prompt: You find a layer of dark ash rich in iron and magnesium. What kind of eruption most likely made it?

options.label: A hugely explosive rhyolite eruption
A low-energy eruption of basalt
A blast of high-silica felsic magma
A violent eruption of dacite magma

items.explain: Low-energy basalt eruptions give dark ash with less silica and plenty of iron and magnesium, while explosive rhyolite gives high-silica ash.
